knowledge_point.title: Integrating a Quotient of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities

question.:question/worked-solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
-1\left(\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}{\sin ^{2}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x\right)=-1\left(\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x\right)
$$

We then use the fact that $\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}=\operatorname{cot}⁡4x$ and $\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}=\operatorname{csc}⁡4x$ to express this as

$$
-1\left(\int \operatorname{csc}⁡4x\operatorname{cot}⁡4x\,\text{d}x\right)
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=4x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1\left(\int \operatorname{csc}⁡4x\operatorname{cot}⁡4x\,\text{d}x\right)& =-1\left(\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\,\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u\right)\\  & =-1\left(\frac{1}{4}\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\,\text{d}u\right)\\  & =-1\left(-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{csc}⁡u\right)+C\\  & =-1\left(-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{csc}⁡4x\right)+C\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Integrating a Quotient of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities

question.:question/worked-solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
-1\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\cos ^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x\right)=-1\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)
$$

We use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and $\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ to express this as

$$
-1\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x\right)
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\cos ^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x\right)& =-1\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-1\left(\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /4}\right)\\  & =-1\left((\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0))\right)\\  & =-1\left(\sqrt{2}-1\right)\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Integrating a Quotient of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the identity $\tan^2x=\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}$ to rewrite the quotient, distribute, and recognize standard trigonometric integrals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \frac{3 \sin^{3}{\left(x \right)} + 3 \tan^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\sin^{2}{\left(x \right)}}\,\text{d}x &=\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \frac{3 \sin^{3}{\left(x \right)} + \frac{3 \sin^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}}}{\sin^{2}{\left(x \right)}}\,\text{d}x \\ &=\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} 3 \sin{\left(x \right)} + \frac{3}{\cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}}\,\text{d}x \\ &=\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} 3 \sin{\left(x \right)} + 3 \sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}\,\text{d}x \\ &=\left(- 3 \cos{\left(x \right)} + 3 \tan{\left(x \right)}\right)|_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &=\left(- \frac{3}{2} + 3 \sqrt{3}\right)-\left(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &=- \frac{3}{2} + \frac{7 \sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
